# Volume rendering

> Volume rendering makes images of data that fill space (a density, a material, a temperature sampled through a region) rather than of surfaces alone.

_This introduction was written by Claude._

## What a volume is

A **volume** is a function over 3D space, $f(\mathbf{x})$, usually known only at samples. The commonest case, and the core of this encyclopedia, is a **[regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md)**: a 3D array of values in which each cell, a **voxel**, is a small cube. CT and MRI scans, smoke and fluid simulations, cloud textures, Minecraft-style worlds and the occupancy grids of game engines all have this form. A voxel can hold a scalar (density, temperature), a material id, a color, or a single occupancy bit [G].

The same ideas carry over to other sampled fields: **hierarchical and adaptive grids** that store detail only where it is needed (octrees, [VDB](#1508-openvdb-vdb.md), [adaptive mesh refinement](#5344-adaptive-mesh-refinement-amr-data-structures.md)), **unstructured meshes** of tetrahedra and other cells, **implicit fields** such as signed distance functions that are evaluated on demand, and **learned fields** such as [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) and 3D Gaussians [G].

## Two ways to draw a volume

**Extract a surface, then draw the surface.** Choose a level $f(\mathbf{x}) = c$ (an **isosurface**) or the boundary of the solid voxels, turn it into triangles, and draw them with an ordinary GPU pipeline. Most voxel games and many medical viewers work this way [G].

**Render the volume directly.** Treat the data as a semi-transparent medium and add up its contribution along each viewing ray. This is **[direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md)**, introduced in its common form by Levoy [S16] and by Drebin, Carpenter and Hanrahan [S3]. Everything from medical CT viewers to film clouds to neural radiance fields is a variant of it [G].

## The volume rendering integral

Along a ray $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\,\mathbf{d}$ through a medium with extinction coefficient $\sigma(t)$ and emitted color $c(t)$, the color that reaches the eye is [S20]

$$C = \int_0^{D} T(t)\,\sigma(t)\,c(t)\,dt, \qquad T(t) = \exp\!\Big(-\int_0^{t} \sigma(s)\,ds\Big)$$

$T$ is the **transmittance**: the fraction of light from depth $t$ that survives to the eye. Max [S20] surveys this [emission–absorption model](#927-emission-absorption-model.md) and its relatives. Renderers approximate the integral by taking samples every $\Delta t$ and **[compositing](#2436-compositing.md)** them, usually front to back so that a ray can stop as soon as it is nearly opaque (early ray termination) [S17, S20]:

$$\alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\sigma_i \Delta t}, \qquad C \leftarrow C + T\,\alpha_i\,c_i, \qquad T \leftarrow T\,(1 - \alpha_i)$$

**Classification** turns raw data values into $\sigma$ and $c$, usually through a **transfer function**: a lookup table from value (and sometimes gradient magnitude) to color and opacity [S13, S16]. The same two formulas drive [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) and [Gaussian splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md); only the source of $\sigma$ and $c$ changes [S21, S12].

## The ten branches

The encyclopedia is a tree. Its root is this page; below it are ten branches, ordered from the data, to the ways of drawing it, to what it is used for.

### 1. [Volume data and representation](#=Volume_data_and_representation)
How a volume is held in memory. Dense grids are simple but large, so layouts such as [bricking](#914-bricking.md) and Morton (Z-order) curves keep neighbouring voxels close in memory [G]. Real volumes are mostly empty or uniform, so **[sparse structures](#5-sparse-structures.md)** store only the occupied parts: [octrees and sparse voxel octrees](#=Sparse_Voxel_Octrees), [sparse voxel DAGs](#=Sparse_Voxel_DAG), which merge identical subtrees (Kämpe, Sintorn and Assarsson [S10]), and [VDB](#=OpenVDB), the shallow, wide tree used in film production (Museth [S23]). The branch also covers [value compression](#6-value-compression.md), levels of detail, out-of-core streaming of data larger than memory, non-regular meshes, and neural and [Gaussian representations](#5918-gaussian-based-representation.md) [G].

### 2. [Producing volume data](#=Producing_volume_data)
Where volumes come from: [voxelization](#=Voxelization) of triangle meshes and point clouds, procedural fields built from noise and distance functions, measurement by CT, MRI, microscopy or seismic surveys, and the output of fluid, fire and astrophysics simulations [G].

### 3. [Image-order rendering](#=Image-order_rendering)
Methods that start from the pixels and cast a ray per pixel. [Volume ray casting](#=Volume_Ray_Casting) samples the volume along the ray, interpolates (usually trilinearly), classifies and composites [S16, S17]. To visit exactly the cells a ray crosses, the [3D DDA](#=3D_DDA) of [Amanatides and Woo](#3061-digital-differential-analyzer-dda-traversal.md) [S1] keeps, per axis, the distance to the next cell boundary and always steps across the nearest one; this is the inner loop of most voxel ray tracers [G]. Speedups include [empty space skipping](#=Empty_Space_Skipping) and early ray termination (Levoy [S17]). For surfaces, isosurface [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) stops at the first crossing of a level [G], and [sphere tracing](#=Sphere_Tracing) (Hart [S6]) uses a distance field's value as a safe step size.

### 4. [Object-order rendering](#=Object-order_rendering)
Methods that walk the volume and project each piece onto the screen. [Splatting](#=Splatting) (Westover [S26]) draws each voxel as a small blurred footprint; [3D Gaussian splatting](#=3D_Gaussian_Splatting) (Kerbl et al. [S12]) applies the same idea to millions of fitted Gaussians. [Shear-warp](#=Shear-Warp) (Lacroute and Levoy [S15]) shears the volume so that its slices line up with the image. [Texture slicing](#25-texture-slicing.md) draws many blended, view-aligned polygons and was the [classic](#5024-classic-column-voxel-space.md) way to run volume rendering on early GPUs [G]. [Cell projection](#26-cell-projection.md) draws unstructured meshes one tetrahedron at a time ([Shirley and Tuchman](#877-projected-tetrahedra.md) [S25]), and Fourier volume rendering computes projections in the frequency domain (Malzbender [S19]).

### 5. [Surface extraction](#=Surface_extraction)
Turning a volume into a mesh. [Marching Cubes](#=Marching_Cubes) (Lorensen and Cline [S18]) looks up triangles for each cell from the signs at its eight corners; [dual contouring](#=Dual_Contouring) (Ju et al. [S8]) places one vertex per cell and keeps sharp features. Blocky worlds instead emit the visible faces of solid voxels and merge them with [greedy meshing](#=Greedy_Meshing) [G].

### 6. [Light transport in participating media](#=Light_transport_in_participating_media)
The emission–absorption model above ignores light that scatters inside the medium. Physically based renderers add shadows within the volume, phase functions, and [single and multiple scattering](#35-single-and-multiple-scattering.md), usually solved by Monte Carlo methods such as delta (Woodcock) tracking [S24]; Kajiya and Von Herzen [S9] gave an early formulation and Novák et al. [S24] survey the field. Real-time renderers approximate this with froxel grids (Hillaire [S7]) and [voxel cone tracing](#=Voxel_Cone_Tracing) (Crassin et al. [S2]).

### 7. [Visualization mapping](#=Visualization_mapping)
Making a picture that explains the data, not only one that looks right. The core tool is the [transfer function](#=Transfer_Function); [multi-dimensional transfer functions](#=Multi-Dimensional_Transfer_Function) also use gradient magnitude and other derived values to separate materials that share a data value (Kindlmann and Durkin [S13]; Kniss, Kindlmann and Hansen [S14]). The branch also covers multi-field, vector and tensor data, illustrative and non-photorealistic styles, and [interaction](#41-interaction.md) such as [clipping](#1444-clipping.md) and focus-plus-context views [G].

### 8. [Differentiable and inverse volume rendering](#=Differentiable_and_inverse_volume_rendering)
Running rendering backwards: given images, find the volume that produced them. Because the volume rendering integral is differentiable, its parameters can be fitted by gradient descent [S21]. [Neural radiance fields](#=Neural_Radiance_Fields) (Mildenhall et al. [S21]) fit a network that returns $\sigma$ and $c$ at any point; [Plenoxels](#=Plenoxels) (Fridovich-Keil et al. [S5]) and [Instant NGP](#=Instant_NGP) (Müller et al. [S22]) store the parameters in voxels or hash tables to train far faster. Tomographic reconstruction, as in CT, is the classic inverse problem of the same kind (Feldkamp, Davis and Kress [S4]).

### 9. [Systems and applications](#=Systems_and_applications)
Where the methods are used, linking back to the branches above: [voxel engines and games](#47-voxel-engines-and-games.md), film production (VDB pipelines, clouds, fire), scientific and medical visualization, [GPU, web and parallel renderers](#50-gpu-web-and-parallel-renderers.md), and [volumetric displays and holography](#51-volumetric-displays-and-holography.md) [G].

### 10. [Elementary building blocks](#=Elementary_building_blocks)
The small pieces that volume renderers are built from: ray–box intersection by the slab test (Kay and Kajiya [S11]) and other [ray–primitive tests](#769-ray-primitive-intersection.md), camera models that generate the rays, and [parallel GPU primitives](#771-parallel-and-gpu-primitives.md) such as atomics, prefix sums, sorting and stream compaction [G].

## Where to start

- **Render a CT scan or a smoke simulation:** [volume ray casting](#=Volume_Ray_Casting), then [transfer functions](#=Transfer_Function) and [empty space skipping](#=Empty_Space_Skipping).
- **Build a blocky voxel game:** [greedy meshing](#=Greedy_Meshing), then the [voxel engines](#=Systems_and_applications) in branch 9.
- **Ray trace huge voxel scenes:** [3D DDA](#=3D_DDA) [S1], [sparse voxel octrees](#=Sparse_Voxel_Octrees), then [sparse voxel DAGs](#=Sparse_Voxel_DAG) [S10].
- **Extract smooth surfaces:** [Marching Cubes](#=Marching_Cubes) [S18], then [dual contouring](#=Dual_Contouring) [S8].
- **Render clouds and fog:** [light transport in participating media](#=Light_transport_in_participating_media).
- **Reconstruct a scene from photographs:** [neural radiance fields](#=Neural_Radiance_Fields) [S21], then [3D Gaussian splatting](#=3D_Gaussian_Splatting) [S12].
